summary: Sets out the Internet best current practice for assigning entries under URI.ARPA, the domain used by the DDDS system for URI resolution. It is part five of the DDDS series. It was later updated by RFC 8958.

eli5.summary: A special place in the internet's address book holds the lookup rules for web-style names. This document says who may add entries there and how.

subtitle: The rules and mailing-list process for adding resolution rules to the URI.ARPA and URN.ARPA DNS zones.

tldr.problem: DNS-based URI resolution starts by looking up a rule in the URI.ARPA zone (or URN.ARPA for URNs), so there must be a controlled way to decide who may add those rules and what they may say.
tldr.mechanism: A rule (a NAPTR record) can only be added after its URI scheme or URN namespace id is properly registered. A template is sent to an open mailing list, and if nobody raises a DNS-related objection within two weeks, IANA enters it.
tldr.outcome: Registrations are tied to the existing scheme and namespace processes and rules with changeable data are expected to point to less stable zones. The RFC is a Best Current Practice and is updated by RFC 8958.

today: RFC 3405 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 65). The unit metadata shows it is updated by RFC 8958, so read that RFC alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What URI.ARPA Is For
sections.content:
This is part five of the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) series, which is specified in RFC 3401. The RFC says it is impossible to understand any document in the series without reading the others. It defines the policies and procedures for inserting Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) records into the URI.ARPA and URN.ARPA zones, which are used to resolve Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) with the DNS-based DDDS database.

The first step of resolution is to append URI.ARPA to the URI scheme and fetch the NAPTR record for that name. For example, resolving http://foo.com/ starts with a lookup of http.URI.ARPA. URN resolution follows a similar procedure but uses URN.ARPA as its root.
sections.eli5: To find out how to open a web-style address, a computer first looks up its type, like http, in one special directory. This document is about who may write in that directory.

sections.title: URI Resolution versus URN Resolution
sections.content:
The initial instructions, called hints, for DNS-based resolution of URIs are stored as resource records in the URI.ARPA zone. A URN is itself a URI scheme, so the hint for the prefix urn: also lives in URI.ARPA.

That rule says to extract the namespace id, append URN.ARPA to it, and use the result as the key for the next NAPTR lookup. So URNs take two hops: first URI.ARPA, then URN.ARPA.
sections.eli5: For one kind of name, the first directory just says to look in a second directory. Two lookups instead of one.

sections.title: Registration Policies
sections.content:
Creating a URI scheme or URN namespace id (NID) follows the documents for those spaces: RFC 2717 for URI schemes and RFC 2611 for URN namespaces. The NAPTR record comes second. A record in URI.ARPA MUST NOT precede proper registration of the scheme and publication of a stable specification, and the scheme MUST be in the IETF URI tree. The IESG or its designated expert reviews for correctness and technical soundness, consistency with the published URI specification, and that the record does not hand resolution of a DNS-based URI to anyone other than the holder of the DNS name, which would risk hijacking traffic.

The URN side mirrors this: a record in URN.ARPA MUST NOT precede proper NID registration, so that it cannot circumvent that process. In both zones a request MAY accompany the scheme or NID request and be reviewed at the same time, or be submitted afterwards. If someone other than the IETF controls the specification, the IESG will require approval from its owner or maintainer first. For URNs, this applies to all NAPTR records for a NID, even if a record affects only part of the namespace.
sections.eli5: You cannot put your name in the directory until you are properly signed up in the club. And if the club rules belong to someone else, you need their permission first.

sections.title: Requirements on Hints
sections.content:
Delegation of a namespace happens in two ways. For most URIs the key to delegate to is hard-coded into the identifier, such as a hostname in an HTTP URI. In other cases the new key can be part of the hint itself.

To keep query load on the two zones low, the RFC anticipates that records there will have extremely long times to live (TTLs), perhaps measured in years. So when the resolution hints for a prefix or namespace are likely to change, the real rule should live in a less stable DNS zone, and the URI.ARPA or URN.ARPA record should be a stable NAPTR that points there.

The RFC gives two examples. The foo URN namespace has flexible rules, so its record points to a name server with a shorter TTL. The http scheme has a fixed syntax in which the host to ask is in the URI, so its rule can sit directly in URI.ARPA.
sections.eli5: The main directory is rarely updated, so it should only hold things that never change. If something changes often, the directory just says where to find the up-to-date answer.

sections.title: Submission Procedure and Template
sections.content:
Following the model of the MIME content-type registration process, a request template is submitted to an open mailing list of interested parties. If no objections are made within a two week period, a representative of the registration authority treats the submission as accepted and enters it into the name server. Requests go to register@URI.ARPA or register@URN.ARPA, and the registration authority is the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

Objections are limited to impacts on the zone itself or on DNS in general. Objections to the scheme or namespace id are not allowed, as they belong in their own forums. Therefore any sanctioned URI scheme or URN namespace MUST be allowed to register if it meets the rules on times to live and general impact on DNS.

The template MUST contain a Key (the NID or URI scheme, used as the domain portion of the DNS entry), an Authority (the individual or organization with authority to register the record, either the IESG or an authority named in the scheme or NID registration), and the Records (the DNS records, with Preference, Order, Flags, Services, Regex and Replacement as defined in RFC 3404). The RFC also supplies the template for the urn rule itself in the URI.ARPA zone.
sections.eli5: You fill in a short form saying the name, who you are, and the rule. It is posted publicly. If nobody can point out a real technical problem in two weeks, it goes in.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has created the URN.ARPA and URI.ARPA zones. The only names assigned within them are the keys described in the template, IANA manages the zones' administration and operation, and the records are subject to the review process of this RFC. IANA has also created the two discussion lists and manages them.

The security section warns that the two zones will be a common point of attack, both for denial of service and for spoofing entries in order to redirect delegation paths. Anyone running name servers that hold these zones should secure them as an infrastructure-level component of the Internet, and should sign the records once a name server can reliably do so.
sections.eli5: Because everyone relies on this directory, it is a tempting target. Whoever looks after it has to guard it well.

data.title: A delegating rule and a fixed-syntax rule
data.code:
foo     IN NAPTR 100 10  ""  "" "" urn-resolver.foo.com.
http    IN NAPTR 100 100 "" ""  "/http:\\/\\/([^\\/:]+)/\\2/i" .
